rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. This establishes the elution window for subsequent slope and temperature optimization.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether that score can be maintained with faster elution, while isolating the effect of gradient slope.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the full-resolution speed limit and quantify the critical pair’s slope sensitivity. Injection 2 remains a maximum-score fallback if resolution drops below 1.5.

Keep the gradient fixed and test higher temperature for a selectivity shift that could restore the critical pair’s resolution while shortening retention. Injection 2 remains the faster verified method with maximum CRF.

Return to the shortest verified fully resolved gradient and test a moderate temperature increase to accelerate elution. This may improve the middle pair’s separation without the early-pair co-elution seen at 60 C.

Trim the gradient window around the observed elution range and shorten its duration, keeping the slope close to injection 5’s fully resolving slope. This tests faster elution while retaining resolution of the critical middle pair.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward and trim the endpoint while preserving approximately the fully resolving slope of injection 6. The last peak is expected to remain inside the gradient, with faster elution and a modest resolution margin.

Raise the gradient window by one grid step while keeping slope and temperature fixed to shorten retention further. Check whether the early pair and critical middle pair retain R ≥ 1.5 as initial retention decreases.

Make the gradient one step shallower to restore the middle pair’s resolution, which narrowly missed 1.5 in injection 8. This should preserve much of the time saving from the higher starting organic fraction.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while retaining the endpoint, combining faster initial elution with a shallower gradient to protect the middle pair. Monitor the early pair for compression as it approaches the dead time.

Test a faster, steeper gradient at low temperature to explore whether the critical middle pair separates again after reversing elution order. Lower temperature should also protect the early pair from the compression observed at high temperature.

Test a higher starting organic fraction on the fast, low-temperature branch to shift middle-pair selectivity. The narrower gradient window also reduces slope, which may improve the late pair’s resolution.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction shifts the unresolved middle pair’s selectivity on the low-temperature branch. The shallower slope should protect the late pair, while the early peaks must be checked for excessive compression.

Test a narrower, higher-starting window to strengthen the middle pair’s separation on the low-temperature branch. This deliberately probes the initial-retention limit; the early pair must remain resolved despite the first peak approaching dead time.

Hold starting composition and temperature fixed while reducing slope to test whether the remaining middle-pair deficit can be recovered. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition in injection 14, limiting the risk of excessive hold retention.

The middle pair barely improved when slope decreased, so test a temperature-driven selectivity change instead. Relative to injection 14, change only temperature by one step while retaining its faster gradient.

Test a steeper gradient at an intermediate temperature for separation on the reversed-order branch of the middle pair. The lower starting fraction than injection 16 should preserve early-pair retention, while the strong endpoint ensures rapid complete elution.

Return to the maximum-score region and test a two-minute gradient with a shallower slope to protect the middle pair. The last compounds will likely elute during the hold, so this tests whether a shorter programmed gradient can retain full resolution without exceeding ten minutes.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to shorten the fully resolved method while protecting the middle pair. Lowering temperature slightly may preserve early-pair separation as initial retention decreases.

Use the six-minute grid to obtain a slope between injections 8 and 9, targeting full resolution with faster elution than injection 9. The predicted middle-pair resolution is just above 1.5, while the early pair should retain its margin.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a slightly shallower gradient near injection 9 to increase the critical-pair resolution margin. This should retain complete elution well within ten minutes while providing a more robust maximum-score method.

Refine around injection 10 by lowering the endpoint one step to improve its narrow middle-pair resolution margin. This should provide a maximum-score method faster than injection 21, with better resolution margin than injection 10.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 10 to test the speed limit around the fastest verified maximum-score method. The middle pair is at risk of falling below 1.5; injection 10 remains the fallback if this steeper gradient sacrifices resolution.

Back off from injection 23’s excessive slope using a grid combination slightly shallower than injection 10. This targets full resolution with a little more margin than injection 10 and faster elution than injection 22.

Use the final injection to test temperature sensitivity around injection 22’s fully resolved method, changing only temperature by one grid step. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 10 remains the fastest verified method achieving it.
